title: Remember me
author: Advi
content:
Oh, I'm floating,  
floating in blue.
My bare skin is engulfed in your blue.
If I become a stone within flowers,
oh dear, forget me not.
Remember me time to time—
but not enough to consume your time.
Don't look for me,
yet you will find me in the sun
that shines through your glasses.
You'll find me in the daisies that bloom on graves.
You'll find me in the trail of salty water
that flows down your cheeks.
Oh, you'd surely find me in the cats that cross your path.
Or maybe I'd just be present
in your far-off memory—
'cause never in your heart.
Remember me time to time—

but not enough to lose track of time.
Just enough to forget me not.
'Cause I'd not forget you,
even when I die.
Not when my lungs are filled with maggots.
Oh, wouldn't they be surprised
when they reach my heart?
To find out it's not mine,
As much it is yours.
But if you ever step onto the grounds
that I've been buried in...
oh, they would know.
They would know whom my soul craved for.
And they'd gaze in awe.
They'd gaze with love
the way I had gazed once upon a time through my blurry eyes.
They would realise
that death didn't salvage my pain.
They would realise

it only prevented more from coming.
Remember me time to time—
but not enough to make you visit me.
'Cause I'm afraid you might feel
the hint of pain you had caused me.
You might feel the agony
you put me through.
Oh dear,
How oblivious could you be?
To hurt me?
The honey you've given me with your poison,
Has killed me
Remember me time to time—
but not enough to forget time.

title: have you ever thought about your mother's dreams at your age?
author: Samiha
content:
have you ever thought about your mother's dreams at your age?
to enunciate what my mother's life could've been, and an attempt at minimizing my inescapable guilt

To start, the title is one of those quotes that made me want to rip my throat out, the first time i read it. Every once in a while, I’ll ponder and stumble across the thought, what about my mother’s dreams when she was just 23? Knowing her, i know she must have had dreams in which she wanted to become someone, have a say of her own. But instead, she got married, became a wife, and then became a mother; a mother of the kids who will never be able to compensate or repay her for her altruism. As i write this, i can’t help but pause to clear my mind off of the guilt, shame, and regret for all the times i’ve been nothing but disrespectful, apathetic, and ungrateful towards her and her awful amount of sacrifices, around which our lives are built. The woman who left her home, hopes, and dreams to build a home for herself; my mother, who deserves the world and nothing less. Yet, i can’t even give a mere act of selflessness.

“either a mother and daughter know each other very well or they are strangers.”
To encapsulate the words i’ll never end up confessing to her, this is my small attempt of pouring out the words of this piece of writing, and for the words that struck me to the point where i had to stop and stare. Such as that one quote i read, somewhere down the rabbit-hole of the internet, that my thoughts keep circling back to:
“the world is not like your mother, you won’t storm off in her face in the morning and expect a dinner meal awaiting you on the table at the end of the day, the world will leave you starving”
And to end my unending rambling and use others’ words to fill the absence of my own, some of the quotes from one of my favorite books, “please look after mom” by Kyung-Sook Shin—the piece of media that actually started my endless loop of spirals—are filled within this piece of writing that i’m too cautious to call an article.
“to you, mom was always mom. It never occurred to you that she had once taken her first step, or had once been three or twelve or twenty years old. Mom was mom. She was born as mom. Until you saw her running to your uncle like that, it hadn’t dawned on you that she was a human being who harbored the exact same feeling you had for your own brothers, and this realization led to the awareness that she, too, had had a childhood. From then on, you sometimes thought of mom as a child, as a girl, as a young woman, as a newlywed, as a mother who had just given birth to you.”
A part of me will always wonder about the life she could’ve led, only if she didn’t have the burden of ours; only if she had the chance of pursuing her dreams, the things that make her happy.
“...i have so many dreams of my own, and i remember things from my childhood, from when i was a girl and a young woman, and i haven’t forgotten a thing. So why did we think of mom as a mom from the very beginning? She didn’t have the opportunity to pursue her dreams, and all by herself, faced everything the era dealt her, poverty and sadness, and she couldn’t do anything about her very bad lot in life other than suffer through it and get beyond it and live her life to the very best of her ability, giving her body and her heart to it completely. Why did i never give a thought to mom’s dreams?
The woman who raised me, created the home I call my own, yet the one I was always so hesitant and distant with to show my love, admiration to. The one I was supposed to be in debt my whole life, yet the one who always somehow got the worst of me.
“did mom know? That i, too, needed her my entire life?”
This is for the woman who made me the person i am today; i hope i become even a fraction of the woman that you are, and i hope you’re happy, ammu.

title: The Script of a Life: The K-Pop Industry
author: Charlotte Diane
cover: /images/articles/submissions/TMD-20261012-235316-6591_The Script of a Life The K-Pop Industry (1).png
content: The Script of a Life: The K-Pop Industry The connections people feel with celebrities, with artists and influencers are very real. But what if the very thing they love is simply a persona—a facade? If you’ve read “The Last Answer” by Isaac Asimov, you’ll know what I’m talking about. Asimov, who was considered the king, perhaps even the godfather of science fiction, first published this short story in the January 1980 issue of Analog Science Fiction and Fact. Forty-five-year-old physicist Murray Templeton dies in his lab due to a heart attack and wakes up in a daze, noticing that he was watching the scene in the lab from above. His vision starts fading as darkness consumes him, and he sees a vague human figure in the last glimmer of light. The Voice reconstructs him and brings him back to life as a source of His entertainment in a universe entirely under His control. Murray’s purpose? It’s to think. To think for eternities and discover new knowledge. The Voice constructed this universe, life, and minds because He wants a surprise—something random, something erratic. The trap? Murray cannot destroy himself, as the Voice will simply adjust the nexus, remove the option that finished him, and bring him back. “The Last Answer” not only predicted the modern world, but specifically the entertainment industry. The similarities between the story and the entertainment industry can only be viewed if looked at the broader picture. Murray Templeton is a victim. His ending was stolen from him for the sake of entertainment. He has no freedom except for what the Voice allows him. No choice, no decisions. He’s merely a puppet—a mere pawn in the Voice’s cruel game. Now, look at the artists of the entertainment industry. It has been proven countless times how cruel the show business is, how inhumanely the companies treat their artists. If an artist does something wrong, people jump to hate. Yet the companies are the ones controlling every decision. Every single move is pre-planned. The companies are brilliant masterminds. They found the perfect path to limitless money. I would like to turn to the K-Pop Industry to show evidence. It’s all a game of psychology. From my perspective though, it’s even worse for Korean artists because, unlike the Western industry, they’re called idols. They’re quite effectively manufactured to be worshipped—to be idolised. Furthermore, not only is sexualization very common in this industry, but the sexualization of minors is through the roof here. Female groups with minors are often given clothes without

proper coverage, provocative choreographies, and lyrics with clear sexual innuendo. 5th gen group BABYMONSTER’s company, YG, has faced scrutiny many times due to the nature of some choreographies with minors Rora and Chiquita, alongside the group’s performance outfits, which managed to bring a massive wave of criticism towards their stylists. 4th gen group NewJeans’ company ADOR faced intense backlash back in August 2022 due to the sexual nature of the lyrics from the song ‘Cookie.’ At the time, the youngest member, Hyein, was 14. Other members—Haerin was 16, and Danielle and Hanni were 17, leaving only Minji to be an adult. Even then, she was just 18. Not only do companies not protect minors, but they also actively sexualise them to bring in more fans. The companies also very clearly push parasocialism to generate more revenue. The most widely known group, BTS, is going into their 30s, yet they cannot admit they have had partners, as it would cause millions of damage in stock due to the nature of their relationships with their fandom, ARMY. Even Stray Kids, a group known for its authenticity and creative freedom, falls into this category. The artists cannot be blamed either because they're victims too. They're more of a victim than the fans are. Most people decide to become trainees in their early teenage years, around 13, with some even making it as early as 8-10. They don't understand the industry, the issues. Neither do their parents. Their parents think they're sending their kids off to somewhere safe and nurturing, but it's the complete opposite. Every little movement, every line, every outfit is controlled by the companies. Murray is the puppet in the story, and The Voice is the puppeteer—the mastermind. The Voice is the employers, the money-hungry companies. The artists don't have any control over their lives when they sign the contracts. They essentially sell their souls. In the end, idols are just slaves of an industry that preys upon innocent children. Companies pre-plan everything. Before debut, the members are presumably evaluated, and their personalities are amped up to 100 to get maximum attention from fans. Members like Chan, Hyunjin, and Felix get the most focus because they’re openly affectionate towards fans, meaning they generate more attention. More attention means more interest; fans will buy more of their merch as they feel validated, hence more attention means more revenue for the company. This brings me to a theory I have regarding Lee Know. He is my bias, and he's been my role model since I was 11. Throughout my time in the fandom, I've consistently seen him get ignored by the company. So my question is—

What if the company ignores him due to his flawless professionalism? Lee Know, whose birth name is Lee Minho, is the perfect employee. He keeps his head down and treats being a K-Pop Idol strictly as a 9-5 job. He has strict boundaries to protect his mental health, because that is the only aspect of his life that is in his control. Everything else has already been curated to fit the image the company chooses for him. Due to his bluntness and refusal to put up an act (except for what is generally needed), many fans find him rude at first glance. Even when he really isn't. So what if the company intentionally ignores him because he refuses to do anything more than absolutely needed, as specified in the contract? He does not do fan-service. So the company keeps the focus on the more loving guys like Chan, Hyunjin, and Felix. Members who will keep the parasocialism alive. I am not saying they do not speak out; they do. Chan leads STAYVille (STAY=Fandom Name) like a military. If he sees something is wrong, he speaks up and scolds fans on the paid chat service, JYPE Bubble. But that does not mean they do not generate “boyfriend content” to create unhealthy relationships. Which, furthermore, fuels an obsession. Obsession means parasocialism. And, going back to my previous point, parasocialism means more revenue. However, Lee Know has definitely built his loyal fandom due to his blunt honesty and “4D personality” (quirkiness). He is adored due to his catlike mannerisms and feline beauty. Aside from that, he is a philanthropist, known for actively sponsoring children domestically and internationally through the World Vision Project and donating to cat shelters and hospitals. Lee Know was officially named the youngest member of World Vision’s esteemed “Bob Pierce Honor Club” on February 28, 2024. Lee Know immediately contributed to emergency relief efforts following the devastating Turkey-Syria earthquake in February 2023. Though this is less well-known, Lee Know also participated in the 18th "Love Your W" Breast Cancer Awareness Campaign, alongside member Felix, starring in digital promotional videos holding the iconic "Love Your W" charity art mugs. Lee Know has also worn accessories to spread awareness. He has been spotted wearing an earring of a polar bear from the Tear of Glacier collection from the Korean jewelry brand Wing Bling multiple times. A percentage of every purchase is donated to the World Wide Fund for Nature, which supports the conservation of endangered species. He has also worn another earring that supports the conservation of snow leopards from the same brand. He has mentioned the cause in live broadcasts.

In August 2019, Lee Know famously engaged fans through the official Stray Kids Twitter account, sharing a photo to ask for their input on which earrings he should wear for the day, showing a safety-pin earring, alongside his snow leopard and polar bear earrings. Safety-pin accessories have a specific meaning: “You’re safe with me,” primarily symbolizing solidarity and signaling that you stand with minorities such as people of color, immigrants, religious minorities, the LGBTQ+ community, the general population of women, and vulnerable individuals. Furthermore, fans feel fondness for him due to his positive mindset. Lee Know promotes balanced, normal eating habits over restrictive idol dieting, emphasizing strength over body aesthetics. He is also known for giving fans random yet comforting advice and texts, the best known one being a Bubble message where he says, “You did well, you did well. Even if you just breathed, you did well.” This proves that human connection can still be generated through strict corporate restraints. The corporate neglect contrasts sharply against Lee Know’s genuinely kind nature, causing more fans to notice it. He has gotten reused clothes many times; he has been given almost identical black leather jackets for every comeback, and once he was left without proper security in the airport, allowing fans to crowd him. Multiple times, staff members have made fun of his weight, calling him “Chubby cat,” when he clearly showed discomfort. He has constantly been given outfits that are uncomfortable for him to perform in. As one of the main dancers of Stray Kids, Lee Know prefers comfortable clothes in which he can give the maximum amount of energy to dance in front of his fans. He has also stated he prefers not to show a lot of skin, yet there has been a pattern of stylists giving him showy shirts. At the Governor’s Ball this year, Stray Kids took the stage as headliners. In the 90-degree heat, Lee Know was given black leather pants. Leather provides high thermal insulation, trapping body heat, and as it sticks to bare skin, it has poor breathability. The color black absorbs heat. Lee Know was seen pouring water on his thighs, presumably because he was experiencing heat exhaustion and burning up. The only positive outcome that has come out of the negligence Lee Know faces is that he has avoided fueling parasocialism that is seen in so many other groups. Even now, Lee Know remains a servant to a flawed, inhumane system that has lived for decades without issues. A mere puppet that will be discarded as soon as he’s out of use.
Only now, the cracks are starting to show. And fans are finding out.

title: Dear Mama,
author: Charlotte Diane
content: Dear Mama, Perhaps, you never realized the sheer amount of pride I feel looking at you. Perhaps you never noticed the sparkle in my eyes when I see you laughing. Not a pretentious one, a genuine bubbly one. A laugh that comes from your heart. Loud and uninhibited. As if nothing in the world matters, except for that moment. Perhaps you never realized that I notice. I notice your exhaustion. I notice your endless passion for work because you have us to take care of. I notice your attempts at brushing your pain, your struggles off with a smile. "It's a temporary world, forgive those who have wronged me," you say, but I notice. I notice your struggle in sharing those painful stories even after years, because those are permanent scars. They never faded; you just learned to live with them. You learned to give yourself time and accept the hurt, but you chose to forgive those people time and time again. I know why you do it. I know you want us to forgive them the way you have, because your heart is made of gold. Because in every universe, I know for a fact, that you'd pick us over everything if it meant having to go through the same struggles repeatedly. But, you don't understand, do you? The things you've done for us, the way you've raised us is incomprehensible. It's utterly impressive. You worked day and night, and made sure to provide us with everything we needed and more. You showed endless patience and care towards us, even when we asked the stupidest questions. You were exhausted after working all day, yet you still came home and gave us time, you still talked to us for hours, just so we didn't feel neglected. Yet, you still found the time to make meals for us because you know how dearly we love your handmade food. There is so much you have done for us, mum. Do you really think we would be able to forgive those who have hurt you deeply? title: Allergic to Emotions
author: Charlotte Diane
content: Allergic to Emotions The recent books I’ve been reading feel clinical, emotionless, and utterly robotic—as if the humans who wrote them have never experienced the power of humanity, of emotions and feelings. It seems like they have never experienced what it is to feel joy, grief, or anger. Instead, there’s a rigidity to literature nowadays, as if writing is a chore. Not a passion project, not a career, but something to finish within a deadline. Except that literature is not meant to be this way. Creative freedom exists. There is no limit to what you can write. There is a vastness, a literal abyss for literature. No rules, no instructions. You live by your own ideas, your own designs. Schools have a habit of teaching young learners that vocabulary matters most in composition. You need to expand your vocabulary. Use big and complex words. Words that other people need to Google just to understand the meaning. Use big and complex words for simple things because people need to know that you have an impeccable vocabulary. Except that is not it. Literature is a form of art. To be a writer, you need to have creative literacy. It does not mean you can’t have a good vocabulary; you just need a balance. People confuse sophistry with an impeccable vocabulary. You can sound sophisticated and impressive to other people and still sound humane. As a human, you need to be able to show your humane factors in your writing. You need to be able to show your flaws, your emotions. You need to be able to express and articulate if you want to sound humane. That is the literal definition of creative literacy. I read a few pages of a book that a middle-schooler wrote; kudos to her, it's a big feat. However, using complex words for the most basic of things frustrates me. I know how to write formally, too. But we are humans. Humans have emotions. Being overly formal strips away the layer of emotion, the humane factor. To be a writer is to have the ability to relate to your audience. Show resonance, show humility.

When we read books, we want to feel a connection, a bond between ourselves and the characters, and perhaps the author too. We want to feel the emotions they are feeling, feel the grief, the pain, the joy, whatever it may be; we want that bridge of attachment and correlation. We crave that. A perfectly structured sentence is stripped of its layer of humanity, scrubbed of all flaws. When the grammatical structure and the writing format are strictly formal, it starts to feel stuffy and pretentious at one point, because it feels like your point is to show off your expanded vocabulary. It feels like you have built a wall between us; you let us listen to a certain extent, but you never let it get personal. There’s no intimacy, no shared warmth. It feels like we’re intruders in a story we had no right to know about.

title: The Paradox of Pride
author: Sagnik Saha
content: The Paradox of Pride While people might argue that pride is just simple stupidity and overestimation of one’s prowess, I will stand firm against this claim. Pride is not always a show of idiocy, but sometimes the cloak behind unprecedented power. In my opinion, pride can be utilized in a way that displays split-second decision-making, correct judgment of a foe’s strength, and calculated taunting to throw off the opponent’s focus. Pride manifests itself in many forms. In its brilliant forms, it appears as confidence, self-respect, dignity, ambition, and determination. These aspects of pride inspire people to overcome adversity, pursue excellence, and stand firm in the face of overwhelming odds. However, pride also possesses darker manifestations. It can emerge as arrogance, vanity, hubris, contempt, stubbornness, and delusion. When left unchecked, these forms of pride blind individuals to their flaws and convince them that they stand above all others. When utilized in the right way, pride becomes the key to utter dominance. Battles don’t start physically. Intelligent individuals break down the opponent psychologically before the true exchange of blows or the battle of wits even starts. Dismantling the opponent’s mental defenses before the battle causes their confidence and focus to rapidly decrease. This in turn, causes them to blunder due to rage and loss of control over their emotions. In circumstances like these, the brilliant side of pride is shown. For example, the Lion’s Sin of Pride, Escanor, from the anime of Seven Deadly Sins, perfectly expresses the brilliant and good side of pride. By taunting his enemies and pitying them, he makes them lose their focus. This causes him to utterly dominate every fight and save his fellow sins. On one hand, one can boast to be overly prideful on the outside, causing his foe to underestimate him, while showing his true hidden strength in crucial moments where the enemy becomes overly confident of his dominance. On the other hand, one can use pride to pity and enrage his enemies, causing them to make arrogant mistakes and lose their focus. Another great representation of the brilliant, but cold and calculated side of pride is Sosuke Aizen, from the anime of Bleach. By using his superb intelligence, he coldly predicts the strategies and moves of his enemies in a calculated and slightly prideful nature. This overwhelming control over his opponent’s moves causes them to lose their confidence and act wildly, which leads to utter defeat for them. However, pride is like a double-edged sword. It can also be the cause of downfall for some. On one side, pride can assist an intelligent individual. But on the other side, in the hands of impudent fools, it destroys them from the core. The greatest danger of pride is that its strengths and weaknesses originate from the same source. The confidence that allows a person to stand above others can also blind him to his own flaws. The belief that grants one courage in battle can transform into arrogance when left unchecked. One of the most common ways giants lose to underdogs is because of their overwhelming pride and arrogance, which they express in it’s raw form. In turn, their uncontrolled form of pride acts as a poison against them. A great example of this side of pride is Frieza, from the anime of Dragon Ball Z. Frieza’s overwhelming confidence and pride prevents him from learning from his mistakes and use new strategies to defeat his opponents. He frequently underestimates his foes, believing himself to be always above them. This is the very thing that causes him to lose over and over again, in vain. Too much pride blinds a person and strips them of any of their senses. It causes them to be unable to reason, accept losses and always overestimate themselves. It also makes them incapable of admitting their failures, and preventing him from recognizing his mistakes and learning from them. The best example of the foolish side of pride is Kira, better known as Light Yagami, from the anime of Death Note. He used to be a highly intelligent student who was living the high life till the death note appeared one day. Slowly, the thought of him having the power to decide the fate of anyone made him increasingly more prideful. At one point, he even began to think of himself as a god, which leads to his superiority complex. Eventually, his pride and God complex leads to him being destroyed by himself due to his own arrogance and mistakes.

While I will affirm that pride isn’t always perfect and good for each and every person, I will also not deny the ingenious sides of pride. Even as the part of a deadly sin, pride is sometimes the reason of victory and the lighter that keeps the fire burning in one’s heart. Escanor, despite being the embodiment of one of the seven deadly sins, pride, he was able to use his prowess and pride for the greater good of humanity, overpower the demon clan, and save his friends. This leads to him ultimately sacrificing his life to eradicate the demon clan and save his fellow sins. With his absolute coldness and genius level intelligence, Sosuke Aizen calmly defeats his foes without breaking a sweat by predicting their moves and making them lose their hopes. This is the reason pride is a fascinating trait, which ignites the fire of one’s heart, while at the same time, slowly destroys another from the inside. Pride amplifies a person’s belief in himself. In moderation, this creates confidence, determination, and resilience. In excess, it becomes arrogance, delusion, and self-destruction. Thus, pride itself is neither a blessing nor a curse; it merely emphasizes the qualities already present within a person. Yet, perhaps the matter is not that simple. Why is pride considered a vice and sin by society, when, it is the fuel that keeps the fire inside the hearts of great people burning? Why is pride so socially and morally condemned, when, it is the driving force behind the feats and achievements of world class innovators, rulers, athletes, scientists, scholars and even tyrants? If one takes the time to wonder and dwell upon these thoughts, one can eventually realize, the initial question might not be the actual one. The initial question of pride being good or bad might not be the true one. Perhaps, beneath the multiple layers, the true question might be whether one can control pride so it remains a servant to its master, or does it at one point, always become the one who controls, the master even. At the base, pride usually grants one confidence, determination, resilience to pursue almost impossible tasks. It starts off as the driving force behind enormous achievements. Gradually, success follows one after the other. But, the path of pride might not always be linear. At one point, pride starts blinding the master of his senses, clouds his judgement, and eventually strips him of his common sense even. Before one realizes it, the driving force and servant that once pushed one to success, later becomes the very thing that becomes the new master and starts controlling the path of that person, and eventually leads him to utter failures. So, from this observation, one can realize that pride posseses a very peculiar nature, that is unlike any other ordinary tool. A knife doesn’t become sharper or duller because a master or beginner uses it. A pen does not become more clever or dumber because a intelligent individual or a foolish person wields it But, pride directly amplifies the true nature of a person, beyond the surface nature. The effect of pride entirely depends upon the wielder. Pride does not just amplify the user’s strengths, it also amplifies the user’s weaknesses. So, fools grow dumber and wise people grow wiser. Meanwhile, leaders may have more control and confidence, while tyrants may become grow increasingly blinder to their flaws. Ultimately, pride is not dangerous because of its base nature of being neutral towards all at first. It’s dangerous because it grows with the user. The true query is not that pride might be evil or good or both at the same time, the real question, beyond deep layers of thoughts, might be whether the user can control it to a point of keeping it in check, before it starts becoming the very thing that controls the original wielder. But, this is not the end of this fascinating topic. As, in my opinion, many layers remain unexplored due to its sheer depth. Pride is basically a rabbit hole full of endless paradoxes and questions that remain unanswered till yet, leaving philosophers delving into this topic to search for deeper layers and answer the obscure, unanswered questions.

title: A Letter to You
author: Ash
content: Hey there, Yes, I'm writing to you. You are the intended person. Hello, I'm Hector. Anyways, that's not the pressing matter here. The thing is I need you to remember me. As I'm writing to you, my flesh is melting off my bones from the heat. I have managed to find a place to write for now, I had a pen in my shirt pocket fortunately and few documents crumpled up in my bag. Can't say when the fire will reach here. Michael already jumped off the rig. But I have bleak hope regarding him. Maybe I'll jump from the rig, maybe not. I know this is my end is, maybe my body will cling on to life desperately to survive but I have given up. I can understand Michael's will to survive, he has his kid and wife waiting for him to come home. For me, I have no one to greet me when I return, maybe that's why I have given up. Isn't life funny? Our measly lives truly is less than that of a bug, the irony is that the higher ups are probably scrambling to find a scapegoat to save their skin while ours are melting off. Even in this situation I can't help but laugh. Lamenting now, wouldn't do any good. It's the only fate anyways left for me now. People say, in times of danger even atheists turn to God, but I can't help but resent him even more. I had nothing anyways and he had to take that away from me too. I was living somehow, it was my only solace that I existed. I knew I wouldn't even be a name after I died but I didn't ask for such a pathetic death. Sorry, my hand slipped. People are trying to rush out of the rig so someone bumped into me. They didn't even have the time to curse me out at my ridiculous doing. I know him, I think. But his face was nearly half burnt. Sorry, I keep on rambling, I should focus on writing the main thing. I'm writing this letter to nobody. As it is going to go up in flames. I don't know why I am writing this letter. I just want to be remembered by someone, something but that is not possible. I'll wrap my ID inside my letter and keep my bag here. Hopefully it survives somehow. Please remember me. Hector.

title: Invisible
author: Ayesha Afroz Kamal
content: “Invisible” Have you ever felt like you are not being noticed? Have you ever imagined being an average girl in school and college? This is not a story but something I want to share. Life is actually not so perfect and I am not perfect either. Not every story is based on imagination, sometimes it's about real life. So it is my imperfect story. I never felt I am good at anything. And I am not. When I was a kid, I was really bad at studying and the students never talked to me and of course being bullied by them was common. Like I said, I am not good at anything or good at looks. Everyday going to school felt like going to hell. I always had to hear the names like “Rabbit Rabbit” but never talked back to them because I actually looked like a rabbit for my ugly teeth. It was true but it still hurt so much. I never had friends. I was the invisible one. I wished I was good at one thing but no I am not. My childhood is something I don't want back. When I was in KG1 I suffered from jaundice so even though I was sick I studied for my final exam. But of course for me everything had to be the worst. My form teacher didn't agree to make me sit for my final exam because I was a bad student and absent in my class because of my sickness. This never hurts me, what hurts me the most was my mom requesting my form teacher just so I could give the exam. She didn't agree. So I had to repeat KG1 again. After passing my KG1 my mom changed my school. I was admitted in class 3 at my new school. My class 3 was not bad but happiness is not forever. I had to suffer a lot from class 4 to class 8. I did not have any friends so being alone was really something that hurt me. Everyday going to class , coming back home with sadness in my heart. My parents never actually knew the ache. In my class 4 even though I was a bad student I improved a lot with the help of my English teacher. And ‘friends’ ? I wanted friends so bad that I had to give them gifts to be my friend. I know at the end they were just for the gifts. Aah life is so unfair right. Every class was a pain. Once I gave a girl a hair clip she accepted my gift but gave it to another girl. Even if I was hurt I never showed. It made me realize that “people who don't appreciate it don't deserve it”. I just wanted to be someone who's actually good at something. I wanted to make my mom smile for me. As I was bad at maths I had to go to “Aloha” to improve my maths skills. But there was a girl who was my mom's friend’s daughter, she was so good at doing calculations so my mom bragged about how good she was. I got jealous so I had to cheat in solving my workbook. But I got caught. My mom scolded me. She never asked me why I did it. She just saw from her eyes but not from her heart. I just wanted to make her feel proud of me even in the wrong way because I didn't have the brain. I just realized that “pain will make a person stronger”. Darkness will go away, light is on the way is what I wished from God. Seeing the first girl's name on the board was something I wished for. I wish I was someone whose name was on first, second, third. Wish people actually clapped for me. But wish is something that'll probably never be fulfilled. Among everyone I had one person who loved me for me, my grandma. Losing my grandma in class 8 really changed me. My grandma was really close to me and she was my best friend. Her absence broke something inside me. From class 9 I started improving. Now after all the hardships I am now a university final year student. The road was broken but I fixed my way. Now I have actual friends. Pain does make people stronger but it'll keep the scar. And my scar was childhood. Invisible is not a bad word. Sometimes being invisible can make a person wait for better friends.

Life is not a rainbow it will give cold and warm days. Fun fact, I am still the average one. Trying means unlocking a new door for your future so giving up is not an option. Everyone is fighting a battle, all we can do is be kind and considerate. “ Being the invisible one is what makes one shine among millions.

title: Who Speaks When No One Wrote It?
author: Pritom Mohajan
content: Who Speaks When No One Wrote It? Imagine you read a short poem on a quiet morning. It has four lines. It describes a grandmother’s kitchen after the power goes out, when the only light comes from a pot of rice steaming on a gas ring: “The rice keeps steaming after the power is gone, and my grandmother counts the spoons by feel, the way she once counted us when we were small, so that no one is left in the dark.” The last line makes you stop and read it again. You feel something close to grief, the good kind that makes you want to call a parent or a sibling. The poem seems to know what it is like to love someone who is getting older. Well, what if no person wrote it? What if a language model produced it in a few seconds after someone typed a short request? No grandmother counted spoons. No child was counted. No kitchen existed, and no power went out in a particular year that someone still remembers. So ask what changed. The words are the same words. The rhythm is the same rhythm. Your eyes moved across the same lines in the same order. Yet something seems to have left the poem. You might feel a little cheated, or you might feel nothing at all and wonder why you ever felt anything. Either way, the poem is now a different kind of object. The real question is who was speaking when the poem spoke to you, and whether anyone was there to speak at all. Roland Barthes argued that the reader is the real place where a text finds its meaning. Machine-written text seems to fit his argument perfectly, because it appears to have no author standing in the way. But I want to argue that this is a mistake. Barthes freed the reader from the author, but machine text removes the author without freeing anyone. A reader cannot judge a text whose intention belongs to nobody. The missing author does not give the reader power. It takes away the one party who could be asked to answer for what the text claims.

Roland Barthes published “The Death of the Author” in 1967. It is a short essay, and it is one of the most cited pieces of literary criticism of the twentieth century. Its target was a habit of reading that was common in schools and in journals. Critics would read a novel or a poem and then go looking for the author’s life to explain it. If a poem seemed sad, the critic would find the poet’s sad years. If a novel seemed to hide a secret, the critic would dig through letters and diaries for the secret’s source. In this approach, the author was the key that opened the text. Once you knew the author’s intention, you thought you knew what the text meant. Barthes thought this approach was wrong. He wrote that a text is made of many writings, drawn from many cultures and set in conversation with each other. Its meaning does not come from a single origin. In his words, “the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.” This sentence is the center of the essay, and it is often quoted without its context. Barthes was not claiming that real writers do not exist or that their lives are useless. He was saying that the writer’s intention should not be the final judge of what a text can mean. He also gave a positive idea in place of the old approach. He wrote that “the unity of a text is not in its origin but in its destination.” The text gathers its unity at the point where it is read. A reader brings memory, expectation, and mood to the page. Two readers of the same poem may find two different poems, and neither is wrong. For Barthes, this was a kind of freedom. The reader is no longer a passive student taking dictation from a master. The reader becomes an active maker of meaning. Barthes also described writing itself in a way that matters here. He said that writing is “the destruction of every voice, of every point of origin.” The text is a surface where many sources meet and none of them governs the whole. He wanted critics to stop searching for a hidden owner behind the words and start paying attention to the words and to the reader who receives them. This is an idea worth taking seriously. It asks the critic to be humble about claiming to know what the writer meant. It also gives more room to readers who come from different backgrounds and see things the author never imagined. Barthes did not want to shut down interpretation. He wanted to open it.

The case for machine text begins with that same picture of writing as a surface of many sources. A large language model is trained on a huge body of human writing: books, articles, forum posts, letters, product descriptions, and poems. When it produces a new text, it draws on patterns from all of that material. The output is, in a plain sense, a tissue of quotations drawn from countless places. Barthes used that exact image for literature. A machine seems to be the purest case of it. The machine also seems to have no intention in the way a human writer does. When you read a poem written by a person, you can wonder whether the poet was sad, angry, bored, or trying to impress a teacher. Those questions matter to the old way of reading, and they can distract from the text. With machine text, those questions have no clear answer. There is no inner life to consult. There is no biography to check. The reader is left alone with the words. If Barthes wanted the text to belong to the reader, machine text appears to hand it over completely. Consider how often this situation now arises in ordinary reading. A person searches for a recipe, a medical explainer, a product review, or a news summary and finds text that reads smoothly and sounds confident. There is no name at the top that the reader recognizes. There may be a site, a logo, or a byline that belongs to no real person. The reader is free to take what the text offers and fill the gap with their own sense of what it means. The concrete examples are not hypothetical. In early 2023, the technology site CNET was found to have published dozens of financial explainer articles written with the help of an automated system. Several of those articles contained factual errors, and CNET later issued corrections on many of them. Later that year, Futurism reported that Sports Illustrated had published product reviews under author profiles with invented names and stock photos, where no real reviewer appeared to exist. In both cases, the texts were read and believed by ordinary people who had no way to find the person who had stood behind them. The texts were free of an author in one sense, and the readers were left without a way to check them in another. Seen this way, machine text appears to be the completion of Barthes’s project. It has no author to block the reader, and it offers the reader a field of meaning with nothing in the middle. The reader seems to gain the freedom that

the critic in 1967 wanted to give them. This is why the case is attractive. It is the death of the author without any ceremony, and it looks like progress for the reader. The French philosopher Michel Foucault answered a version of this argument only two years after Barthes. In a lecture given in 1969, later published as “What Is an Author?”, he agreed that the author should not be treated as a simple source of meaning. But he added something Barthes did not stress. He argued that the author is not only a person who writes. The author is what Foucault called an “author function,” a social role that controls how texts are classified, shared, and trusted. Foucault gave a sharp description of this role. He wrote that “the author is the ideological figure by which one marks the manner in which we fear the proliferation of meaning.” In other words, a society that has many possible readings of a text uses the author’s name to narrow them. The name tells us which texts belong together, which ones are serious, and which ones are dangerous or false. The author becomes “the principle of thrift in the proliferation of meaning,” as Foucault put it. Without some limit, meaning would spread in every direction, and no one would know what to believe. Foucault’s point is easy to see in ordinary life. A medical leaflet with no company name, no doctor, and no date would not be trusted, even if the words were clear and accurate. A scientific paper without authors or institutions would be hard to cite. An anonymous legal notice would be ignored by most people, and rightly so, because a law needs a source that can be identified. In each case, the name is not just decoration. It tells the reader what kind of text they hold and how much weight it should carry. This means that readers still depend on something outside the text when they decide what it means and whether to believe it. They look for a name, a publisher, a purpose, or an institution. When the name is missing, they look for another way to place the text. The reader does not stand alone with the words. The reader stands with a set of assumptions about who would produce such a text and why.

Machine text does not remove this need. It only removes the name that would normally meet it. So the reader begins to look for a substitute. They may trust the platform that displayed the text, the website that published it, or the company that built the system. They may assume a human editor checked it, even when no editor did. They may trust the tone of the writing, which is often calm and sure of itself. These are weak replacements for an author, and they can be wrong. But they show that the author function is still working, even when no author exists. Foucault therefore gives a sharper version of the problem. The death of the author did not end the social role the author played. It only left that role empty. When the role is empty, the reader must fill it with guesses, or they must accept whatever the machine offers. Here is my position. The missing author does not free the reader. It leaves the reader with no one to hold responsible for a claim. Barthes’s reader is a reader of pleasure and play. A poem can mean many things, and the reader can enjoy the variety. But many texts are not poems. A text can say that a medicine is safe, that a bridge was inspected, that a candidate took a bribe, or that a historical event happened on a certain date. These are claims about the world. A claim is a kind of promise. It says, in effect, that someone stands behind these words and can be asked why they are true. When a text makes a claim and no one stands behind it, the claim is still on the page, but the promise has nobody to keep it. This is the difference between reading for pleasure and reading for trust. In a poem, a missing author costs us a little. We may enjoy the text anyway. In a news report or a medical explainer, a missing author costs much more. The reader cannot ask the writer what the source was. The reader cannot ask whether the writer checked the number. The reader cannot press the writer to correct a mistake or punish a lie. The reader can only accept the claim or reject it, usually with very little information.

Responsibility is not a cold bureaucratic idea. It is the mechanism that makes trust possible. A journalist who signs a story can be questioned, corrected, challenged in court, or dismissed for dishonesty. An editor who approves a story takes on part of that responsibility. A reader who sees the name of a reporter they have trusted for years has reasons to believe the story, because they know who would pay a price if it were false. Trust is built on a chain of people who can be held to account. Remove the people, and the chain breaks. Machine-written text breaks that chain in two places. The first is the writer. The system that produced the words cannot be questioned in any meaningful way, and it cannot feel shame or accept blame. The second is the publisher. A publication that uses machine text may not disclose it, may not check it carefully, and may not own the errors in the way a human writer would. The CNET corrections show what happens next. The errors were fixed, but the reader who had already acted on a wrong explanation had no one to hold accountable for the harm. The fake reviewers in the Sports Illustrated case were not even a real person who could later say what they had tested. This matters most in journalism. A news story is only useful if the reader can judge how it was made. Was the source a government report, a rumor, or a guess? Did a reporter speak to the people involved? Did an editor review the claim? A machine text can imitate the surface of a news story without any of these steps. Its fluent sentences look the same whether the facts are checked or invented. The reader is left to guess, and the guess is made harder by the very smoothness of the writing. Education is another place where the missing author causes damage. When a teacher reads a student’s essay, the essay is evidence of what the student understands. The teacher asks whether the argument is the student’s own, whether the sources were read, and whether the student can defend the claims in conversation. If the essay was produced by a machine, the evidence is false. The teacher cannot judge what the student learned, and the student has not learned what the grade says they learned. The essay is a text with no one behind it who can be asked to

explain it. In this case, the death of the author does not free the student. It takes away the process that education depends on. Some will say that these are problems of bad actors, not of the text itself. A dishonest writer can always lie, whether a human or a machine. That is partly true. But the old system of authors, editors, and names gave readers a way to tell honest work from dishonest work. It was imperfect, and it failed often. Still, it gave readers something to check. Machine text, used without disclosure, removes that check from the reader’s hands. It makes the lie harder to trace and easier to repeat. So I do not think readers should celebrate the death of the author as a simple gift. Barthes was right that a reader makes meaning, and right that a text should not be closed by a single intention. But a reader who makes meaning from a claim about the world still needs to know where the claim came from. The reader should not be freed from this question. The reader should be given a harder duty, which is to ask who stands behind the words, what they would lose if the words were false, and how the claim can be checked. Barthes’s reader cannot do this alone. They need institutions, names, and a clear line of responsibility, even if those things are imperfect. Return now to the four-line poem about the grandmother and the rice. On the first reading, it moved me, and I think that reaction was real. The image of a family in the dark, held together by a counting that is almost a prayer, is powerful. Nothing in my argument changes that the lines work on the senses and the feelings. Barthes would say that the poem still belongs to me, and that my feeling of grief is the meaning it has for me now. But the argument does change how I read the poem. When I learned that no one wrote it, the grandmother stopped being a person who once counted children in the dark. She became a character invented by a system that had learned how such images are usually built. The line “so that no one is left in the dark” stopped being a moment of love and became a pattern that moves a reader. I can still enjoy the pattern, and I may still feel something when I read it. What I can no longer do is treat the line as a sincere statement from someone who knows what it costs

to keep a family together. There is no one to ask what the line meant to them, and no one who would stand behind it if it were false. That is the loss the missing author leaves behind. Some pleasure may remain, and I do not think that pleasure is worthless. But trust does not move with the words. Trust needs a person, and a person needs to be answerable. When the author is gone and nothing takes the author’s place, the reader is alone with a claim that no one will answer for. That is not freedom. It is a kind of abandonment, and the reader should see it clearly before accepting the words at face value.
