title: To lean to the light
author: Fahmiah Fahreen
content: To lean to the light
Sometimes when the curtains are drawn and the Sun sets to sleep, I remember my
Mumma.
I've lost many past memories; they've turned into a liquefied slurry of sceneries and lights
and faces, swirling around and sometimes dribbling a drop or two into my mind, where it
results in nothing but confusion as I try to recall the full picture in vain.
But Mumma...my Mumma I remember. I feel it would be impossible to forget.
In the morning, when golden beams manage to spill through a gap or two between the
blinds and cut bright wedges around me, an equally brilliant image of her pops in as well:
the way sunlight poured through her canopy to cast various aureate shapes around me,
serving as my playmates for the day.
She was beautiful in all different ways I can imagine, not only the way her viridescent
leaves and weeping aerial roots drooped to the ground like a newly-wed's veil, but also how
she stood her ground, how her vast trunk with the millions of ridges and furrows it had
gained throughout the years protruded from the rough soil into the open sky, enormous
snake like roots meandering their way across the surface, anchoring her in place. My
Mumma was the most magnificent of them all, the queen of that peaceful little patch of
forestry I was born in amidst the bustle of urbanization.
I was only a tiny sprout swaying in between two massive distributary-like roots, peeking
through my mother's leafy awning to get a glimpse of the glassy blue sky above. They would
often mistake me for a mere weed, and I didn't mind, as long as Mumma herself
acknowledged me. She would ruffle her leaves and breathe into mine, saying that I would
grow, grow just like her, higher and mightier, even, until I could touch the clouds, that I
would become the heart of this place we lived in. "Just lean towards the light, " she advised,
as rays poked through her leaves, "Lean to the light, and it'll do the rest."
At first it was just me, and Mumma, and the other plants who called her their queen. Then
came she, one fine autumn morning, as my mother parted her aerial roots and I saw my
baby sister. At dusk, when Mumma's branches would be crowded with those tittering birds,
we would participate in their lively conversation. Sometimes, a bird or two would
tentatively fly down to the damp ground, reach out, and as we conversed, they'd carefully
pick out the miniscule bugs and ticks nestled under our leaves.
Sometimes, now, when the occasional sparrow comes to rest on the veranda, I chuckle at the
memories of those chirpy friends of mine.
My Mumma liked to tell stories, stories of her life and the things she'd seen, heard, felt. Me
and my sister would dedicate our full attention to her as she recounted her time as a
maiden tree, and how the loud city around us was once a serene countryside.
Mostly, we loved hearing accounts of `The People'. "They're magical creatures." Mumma
would muse. "They do unimaginable things, some giving life while others take it away."
The first time I saw "The People" was when I was quite a few months old. They looked like
bamboo sticks merged on a trunk to make five branches, the top one small and getting more
rounded, with a bush atop. They came in different sizes and shapes, like us trees, and they
wore different colors of skins over their trunk and branches. It was peculiar, really.
They came and flashed their flat little devices, making snapping sounds across the
plantation. Mumma stood rigid as they uttered enthusiastic remarks.
I could only catch on to one tiny snippet of it, one I can recall to this day: "The Queen
Banyan".
When they left, I could tell by her features that she was worried about them returning,
despite her assurances. In contrast, Sister was practically bubbling, chattering to the birds
and our neighbours about "The People" in her usual vibrant tones.
Mumma was right. They did return. And that's what made me who I am today.
It was a winter, dry and flaky. Instead of the dense white envelope of fog, the sky was a
sickly grey, streaks of black particulates cutting their way through before showering dust
on the canopy. Then all broke loose. Soil crumbled and dust flew, clogging my senses as the
very earth trembled uncontrollably. I only caught a glimpse of those huge `machines',
bounding in, the noise overwhelming me as it overlapped the shrieks of my neighbours. I
flailed around for Sister, and spotted her place amongst the pandemonium...but she wasn't
there. Gone. Uprooted and flattened by the rollers of the machines. I gazed up at it, and
saw someone behind the screen. "The People".
The same ones who fascinated my baby sister so much.
And all Mumma could do was stand there, holding her ground, as one of the monstrous
things approached.
I don't remember the rest, and I'm glad for that.
The next thing I can recall is rumbling and lurching and pitch-black darkness, a darkness
so consuming it tried to swallow me whole. I think there was a small sliver of murky light
from some corner, but the dark swallowed that too, before gnawing at what now remained
of me.
Then it faded.
I was somewhere else, lined up along with hundreds more of others. It was a humid, fuzzy
atmosphere, the air heavy with a mixtured scent of different flowers, damp soil, fertilizer,
manure, rainwashed bricks, and so much more. All around me were different versions of
me, small and weak and slowly ebbing away. Our roots roughly dug into the crumbly, dry
soil filling plastic container. More of those `People', as they took us from place to place,
ripping, digging, ripping again.
My Mumma. I wondered where she was.
It faded again.
Someone called me that. The one they called my Mumma. "Banyan". It sounded nice. Like
home.
I was somewhere else again.
Roots loosely anchored into the caky soil.
Another word. "Bonsai".
I wondered what that meant.
Someone was gently fingering through my leaves and branches. I caught a glimpse of his
face. One lined with experience. Like Mumma.
The next few days, months maybe, or perhaps years, went like a fast forwarded collection of
reels. I was grown alongside a row of similar plants, in round sepia tobs, surviving on water
that smelt of wrought iron.
We, the lined tobs of plants, never felt very inclined to share our stories. Perhaps because
we didn't remember it. Perhaps we didn't want to.
I knew I didn't.
I wondered where Mumma was.
There was one thing, though. There was light. I remembered what Mumma said.
"Lean to the light."
So I obeyed.
But then it was gone.
I was in a different place. Colder and dimmer.
I had learnt another term. "Human".
There he was, the one with the lines in his face like my mother's.
His gnarled, calloused hands were soft and gentle on me.
For a split second, I felt hope.
Snip.
And a crunch and a small thud as one of my branches landed at my roots.
Why?
Snip again, and again, until it was joined by more, my leaves and branches which had just
seen the light.
Then came the wires.
They curled around what remained of me like the snakes that used to come out during
monsoon, wrapping and bending and binding. Splints all over me.
I had become better at understanding them. Humans. They said I didn't feel the pain.
Which must be true, I didn't even know what pain meant.
But I wished it would be over. I wished I could go back to Mumma, stay in her shade, listen
to her stories. Lean to the light. There was barely any now.
More cutting, wiring. They called it pruning. Said it made me beautiful. Aesthetic.
Needles. Needles and syringes, piercing the loose soil into my roots. I wondered what they
did.
All I had to do was grow. That was it. Grow. Hold my head up high into the sky, like
Mumma. Then they couldn't keep me anymore.
But, I didn't. The tiny sprout by the porch had become quite large now. But I hadn't. I was
still here, in my sepia tob.
I still am now.
They come to see me. Call me beautiful. A natural wonder.
But not with the awe that made their eyes glow when they saw my mother.
I was different. Beautiful, aesthetically pleasing, yes. But not natural. Not my mother.
They try, but they can't hide that unease from their eyes.
I don't blame them.
They have a new word for me now, "Bonsai".
Light is pouring through the window now. Inviting me. Lean.
I try. I really do. But I can't.
I hope Mumma understands. She always did.
I love you.
excerpt: A story about reaching toward light while carrying what darkness has made of you.

title: Silent
author: Abontee Ahmed
content: Silence
Abontee Ahmed
Oh Silence! You are the essence of me. You are the veil upon the face of my Beloved. The worst
trait of silence is that through it, fear and hope vanish. If a human remains silent before his
destiny and utters no complaint, he will have neither fear nor hope.
Before Allah destroys me with sorrow and grief, He will not grant me the treasure hidden within
me. Before He carries me away with a burning flood, He will not lead me to the sea of wisdom. I
am a mirror.
I am a mirror. I am the one who is talkative and distracted. Because I am silent, you do not hear
the cries of my heart. Would that your ears could turn into eyes, so you might see how helpless I
am.
I am like a tree shaking its hands in the wind. I orbit like the moon in the sky. When I am upon
the earth, my orbit carries the scent of soil. I am the color of dust; yet though I am made of dust,
since I hold a sacred spirit within, my orbit is purer, more beautiful than the orbit of the heavens.
O Silence, you are my essence. You are my face.
O Sage, speak! Speak, that I may pray for you; for you speak the truth. For every dawn, when the
time of prayer arrives, I become more beautiful, joyful, exultant, and intoxicated.
So upon myself I swear, I shall never deprive you of my warmth or mirth.
And I ask God that whatever He has decreed for the possessor of my heart, He may grant half of
it to me.
The cup of Truth and the cup of Eternity, the Beloved Himself has given them to me. The beggar
who drinks from that wine becomes a fountain of the sun, a divine light giving drink to the
thirsty.
My throat is parched; I can no longer speak.
I have fallen silent.
O sage of beautiful speech, O dweller of my heart, O star of my joy, speak to me, for you are the
possessor of a voice like Dawood's (AS.) and I am as a mountain uprooted and ruined by divine
command.
Abontee Ahmed
excerpt: A poem of withheld words, distance, and the pressure of what remains unspoken.

title: Amidst
author: Rain
content: Amidst
: If you were a bird, what would you do?
Wouldn't you soar through the sky, high above the mists?
Above the haze, the daze, the clocks on wrists?
Beyond orders and borders, where only peace persists?
: I think I'd like to be amidst.
: Amidst?
: Amidst the flowers, the trees, a gentle breeze.
Witness love, laughter, the caress of cheeks;
Heartbreak, failure, perhaps a kiss.
A tear, a smile, momentary peace.
: Momentary peace?
: We love the beach for the ocean is in reach.
Yet not deserts, for it's not "endless" we seek.
The valleys make the mountains high.
The stars require darkness to shine.
So below the clouds is where I'd choose to fly.
For it's the ups and downs-
Which keep me high.
excerpt: A poem held in the unsettled space between what has passed and what has not yet arrived.

title: The Truth About Confidence
author: Nigar Sultana Arni
content: I believe there's a kid that lives inside everyone. A kid shaped by their environment, the way
they were treated, talked to, cared for. That becomes their default image. No matter how
much their life changes, how many storms they pass through, that is how they see
themselves.
You cannot erase that child. Whether that's a good thing depends entirely on which child you
got.
For some, it's beautiful. They were given the affection they needed during their critical years.
They grow up carrying that image of themselves: happy, carefree, without a second thought.
Now let's come to the ones who didn't have it.
Constantly criticized. Constantly made to feel bad about themselves. Constantly neglected.
What does the kid inside them do?
They become exactly what they're told.
You're not worthy of love. I'm not worthy of love.
You're forgettable. I'm forgettable.
You're not wanted. I'm not wanted.
They grow up too, like any other human. Carrying that child inside them, along with the
words they heard and believed to their core.
And they grow to be...
Wait. Did you think I'd talk about the meek, quiet ones? The ones who never learned to raise
their voices against anything that tries to oppress them?
Well, they exist too. I'm not ignoring them.
But we'll keep them aside for today.
Let's talk about the ones who grow up to be dangerously confident. Who don't seem to care
even if the grim reaper appears in front of them. Who'll carry an entire debate with him, too,
and with unbelievable ease.
Sometimes people look at them and think: where does all that confidence come from?
People admire them. People want to be like them. Compliments are not new to them.
These people are magnetic as hell. There's something that draws others toward them,
something they can't quite pinpoint. But it's addictive. So addictive they can't stop.
So the kid is healed, right? It's getting everything it wanted. Praise. Affection. Attention it
deserved.
You think confidence cured them?
Wrong.
It just learned to wear a different face.
Here's a little thing about confidence. People see it as a magical drug, something that
miraculously cures every negative thought, every criticism you believe to be true about
yourself. You achieve it and voila, insecurity isn't part of your life anymore.
As if you haven't carried these thoughts, these voices, these tears for ages. As if it's that
easy to undo years of psychological pain.
And external validation is of no help. Sure, it can momentarily lift one's spirit. It can even
make someone's day a little better.
Key words: Momentarily. Day.
That kid? It still feels the same.
excerpt: An essay about the stories we tell ourselves when confidence looks effortless from the outside.

title: The Strangers I Knew
author: Zohara H. Khan
content: The Strangers I Knew
Prologue

I have never travelled by myself anywhere, certainly not somewhere as far as Beanibazar. When you come from a sheltered family like mine, travelling with company is always a must, at least a pair of two. Yet, here I was, preparing to journey to my ancestral village. My dada bari. On my own. For the first time.

I shall admit, I was surprised when I first found out about the plan. My dad being the strict and protective man that he is would never let his daughter travel by herself. He never let any of my four elder sisters either, yet here I was. What has changed?

I stared at the back of my father’s head as he scrolled through his phone while reading different articles on our country’s situation. My father, Harun, has always been very good at hiding his emotions. True emotions to be exact. And by emotions, I mean, I have never seen him cry. Being the short-tempered man that he is, I have seen his fits of rage, and I have seen him smile. But the only time I heard about him genuinely being happy was when my eldest sisters, Sharmin and Shumin were born. Perhaps it was the excitement of having his first children, but the stories I heard of the man he was then resemble nothing to the man I know him as. Almost as if they are different people.

Not to forget, those were stories I heard from my mom, not him. My father has never been the talkative one with his children, let alone make idle conversations. True, he has always done his duties as a father, fed us, clothed us, educated us, raised us. Everything a father was meant to do. But I can’t remember the first or last time I had a decent conversation with him.

“Kun shomoi baraoi bai? (When will you leave?)” My mother asked from the kitchen, walking into the room and placing a cup of milk tea before my father without turning her attention to me, but I knew she was addressing me.
“Ou baroi zaimu. (Just in a bit.)” I replied, watching her gracefully roam around the room before perching like a docile bird across from my father.

She was… rather good at concealing her inner thoughts. She, Fathima, always had a smile on her face, but she did have her moments of rage if we were unruly. However, I could never tell what she really thought now and then, and it made me wonder if she ever thought at all. My mistake, she did think; about Ahmed. Her only son.
A lot.

Ahmed was my mothers greatest joy, just like Shireen, my third sister was father’s greatest pride. They may have felt the greatest when they had their first two children, but the favorites were their third and fourth- Ahmed and Shireen. As for my fourth sister Tarin and myself being the last, I wasn’t sure.
I didn’t know what they thought of me.

“The baroi zao ekhon. Baade der oizibo. (Then you better leave now, lest it becomes late.)” Were my father’s words to me, barely looking up from the phone in hand. But I could sense the concern edged in his voice.
I’m sure they loved me, but sometimes I can’t help but wonder if I was something they considered a gift, a choice, or a responsibility.
I pursed my lips before getting to my feet, smiling at them. “Acha. (Okay.)”
Because when you have a total of six children, the excitement of parenthood already disappears by the time the third or fourth child is born, let alone the sixth child.
Turning to look at my parents sitting across from one another, I knew exactly what they were.
The textbook versions of parents.
To be on Your Own

The journey to Beanibazar was definitely not an easy one, especially when one is traveling all the way from the city to the rural village. But I had to make it anyway. Starting from Shaporan I hailed an auto rickshaw that drove me till the bypass road, from where I then hailed yet another auto rickshaw that took me further inside only to drop me off at Gulapgonj. Every time I finished a trip, I found myself releasing a sigh of relief knowing that I was getting closer and closer without getting abducted or harassed. A girl can never be certain.

Yet, my journey was far from over, but close nonetheless. I was close to Narafing, and from here on, I could travel via manual rickshaw, which was the part I was looking forward to the most. Riding a rickshaw all by yourself with the wind brushing past your face as it speeds by was a welcoming thought, especially when it was the rural breeze of nature.
“Kano zaitha? (Where to?)” Asked the driver I had managed to hail. My reply was quick. “Beanibazar sinoin ni? (Do you know Beanibazar?)”
“Beanibazar khe na sine? (Who doesn’t know Beanibazar?)”
Right.
“Beanibazar, Ramdabazar, Sondogram?” My attempts at narrowing down my location was laughable. I was only saying names of places registered in my national ID at this point.
“Khano, point o namba ni? (Do you wish to be dropped on the main road?)”
Alright. Here goes nothing. “Khan’s residence sinra ni? (Do you know Khan’s residence?)”
Imagine my surprise when he said he does. This man was a god sent. I was finally saved from further embarrassment.

From then on, the ride was peaceful. The man took his sweet time riding towards my dada bari, while I leaned back and sighed in relief. I was indeed relieved, to the point I found myself feeling drowsy with leftover sleep.
This was not a wise idea, falling asleep in a rickshaw. But somehow, I found myself being lulled to a peaceful sleep, leaving my fate up to the heavens.

I don’t know for how long I slept, or if I had even slept to begin with. All I can say is I had just brushed my eyelids shut, maybe for a minute, or maybe a second, before I felt the rickshaw come to a stop.
“Afa, utokka. Aicchi. (Sister, wake up. We’re here.)”
Already?
My eyelids fluttered open, and true to his words, we had made it. I was right before the massive gates that led to my ancestral home, where my uncles and aunts were still there.
Only that something didn’t seem… right.
The gate seemed so… new. Like it was newly painted. Yet the paint was chipped, but the gate was in better condition than I had last seen it. And the place-
“Afa, bara dibani? (Sister, the fare?)”
Right. The fare- WOAH!
I almost flinched at the sight of the old man before me. Because up until a moment ago, it wasn’t an old man riding me.
Wasn’t it… a middle-aged man? Or did I get it wrong? Did I not look at his face enough?
But then… the rickshaw…
It was manual.
But I remember hailing a motor rickshaw.
What… is going on? Am I dreaming?
The Face of Unfamiliarity

Everything seemed to become a hazy mess before my eyes. I did not know how I paid the man and began making my way forward. All I knew was that my heart was in my throat, and my senses alert to the very strange and unfamiliar scent around me. Almost like it was… ancient.

Nothing felt familiar in this very familiar place. I remember there used to be a grocery shop outside the gates Dola sasa had made. Did they break it down? I don’t know. But the deeper I went, the stranger it got.
Because now I was finally seeing people around, people I call my family. But for some reason, most of them were… children. There were hardly any adults around.
The sound of laughter and giggles grew louder as I drew closer, making my way to a group of children playing on the mud. At the sight of me approaching them, their smiles faltered.
“H-Hi.” I greeted in English like the fool I was.
Silence.
“Umm, ikta kita Khan residence ni? (Is this Khan residence?)”
More silence. Until one of them turned to whisper something in another ear before they jumped to their feet and just like that, they took off. And all I could think was, did I say something wrong?

The kids were gone. Not just the kids I spoke to, but every other kid around as well. The whole place was vacant, like everyone had disappeared at the sight of me. I had no idea what was going on, or if there were any adults, but I needed to find answers. I needed to know where I was because this was certainly not my home. It looked like my home, but it wasn’t home.

“The renovations in Boro sasa’s house are gone. The study room abbu built in our house is gone too. In fact, the bedroom abbu built for Moulana sasa is gone too! And it was constructed two decades ago!” I stopped wherever I was going with a stomp of my foot, unable to believe what I had just seen. “How did everything disappear in less than a year!?”

And the more I think about it, the more it looks odd. I… could not recognize anyone. No matter how little I may have seen of them, I know who my relatives are! There is no way they all just disappeared into thin air and were replaced by children I never saw over there in my life!
So caught up in my train of thoughts, it takes me a while to realize I’m no longer in the Khan residence territory. I was somewhere else, like a rice field.
“Great. Now where the hell did I-”
Until I saw him. A young boy. In the rice field.

Sitting there all by himself, staring into the distance while being surrounded by cows and calves of all sizes. There he was, all alone in that massive watery field, with nothing but his cattle as company. And he looked so… peaceful.
Who are you? And why do you look so familiar?
I did not have long to dwell on it, because just then, my heart leaped out of my chest.
BANG!
The sound of gunfire.
I would be lying if I said I did not jump out of my skin when the shot was fired, followed by another, and another, until it was non stop.
“W-What… what is… what is going on… I-”
Words failed me, for fear had gripped me so hard I was rooted to my spot, unable to move. Tears burned my eyes making it harder to see, for I had no idea where I was, and now there were gunshots.
Could this day get any worse?
Just as I found myself resigning to my fate, I felt a tiny grip on my arm, yanking me towards them.
“Ino ubai ruilai khene!? Lukao! (Why are you just standing there!? Hide!)” It was the young boy from earlier.

I had no idea who he was, yet I found myself being dragged by him until we were both in the rice field, waist deep, before he sucked a breath and motioned for me to do the same. And like a child, I did as told.
And then, we dived in.
The Boy You Are

I don’t know how long we stayed under that murky water with rice plants all over us, but I knew one thing. The boy never let go of my hand. When we finally pulled up, the gunshots were gone. Like they never happened in the first place.
Was I imagining it? But the boy heard them too. Speaking of-

I coughed out whatever murk I may have swallowed, and so did the boy. But unlike my startled self, the boy looked entirely unfazed, like he was used to these things. But how come? This is the first time I’m hearing about a shootout in Beanibazar.
“Dhuk faiso? (Are you hurt?)”
I turned to the young boy looking up at me with his dark black eyes, unable to form any words. Because the more I looked at him, the familiar it got, until I was looking at someone else entirely.
A sudden gasp left my lips as I remembered something, looking at our surroundings. “T-Thumar gai- (Your cows-)”

But the boy only waved at me dismissively, something I noticed was an elderly gesture which this young man had learnt, before he whistled, and out came his herd from the water, having hidden just like us. Smart.
I smiled at the sight of the boy with his cows despite myself, until a thought struck me, my smile faltering immediately. This scene, I feel like I saw it somewhere. Or more like I heard it.
The boy that hid with his cows whenever there was a shootout.
The boy…
But that was impossible. What I was thinking. It was impossible. It couldn’t be.
I stared at the young boy smiling at his cows, the smile I had seen a handful of times, yet I could always recognize it.

“Dorayona. Itha oe kunoshomoi. (Don’t be afraid. This happens sometimes.)” I heard the boy say, confident in his words like it was not a big deal, or confident that he saved a life. But I could not bring myself to smile with him. For I found my heart shattering for this little boy.
He then went on to say, “Thumar naam kitha? Harigeso? (What’s your name? are you lost?)”

“J-J… Jerin.” I don’t know if I could tell him whether I was lost or not. But I needed to know something. But the boy was already talking, leading his cows out with him. “Kuntha oitho nai. Amar loge ao. Amar babai thumare shahaijjo korba. Thain manshore shahaijjo dein. (Don’t worry. Come with me. My dad will help you. He helps people like you.)”
The boy was already out and making his way towards the route I had come from, further registering my fears to be true. But I had to be sure.
So, I stopped the boy, finally ready to get some answers. “Chele, ami faurilaisi. E-Ekhon… kun bosor? (Boy, I have forgotten. W-What… year is it?)”
The boy looked at me judgmentally, but I couldn’t blame him. I really sounded like an idiot. But he answered nonetheless. And what he answered made my blood run cold.
“Buligeso? Ekhon tho unnisho shottor.”
No…
“Forgotten it? It’s 1970.”
But if one bomb wasn’t enough. He dropped another.
“Ar amar naam chele nai. Amar naam Harun.”
“And my name is not boy. It’s Harun.”
The Man You Become

I ended up following the boy. Following… Harun. He promised me his father was very generous and would offer me shelter till I found my footing or even offer me a job. I didn’t argue. I already knew that.
I already knew what sort of man my grandfather was.

So Harun led me to his house, to… my dada bari. Where I had already come and found it awfully strange with unfamiliar faces. Only this time, there were more adult faces than children, and they gathered around Harun like he was lost. I mean he did survive a shootout.
After that, everything happened in a blur. Someone took the reins of the cows from him, and before he knew it he was surrounded by children around his age. Children I now recognize all too well.

My uncles and aunts. Boro sasa. Gura sasa. Dola sasa. Moulana sasa. Mejo fufu. Suto fufu. Mejo sasa. Suto sasa. All… young children. Boro fufu was the only one missing, perhaps because she was already married.

Then I saw dadi. My dadi, fit and well, rushing to her boy to see if he was unharmed. She was… pretty. I had never seen her like this. The only time I saw her alive was on her deathbed. And then she died.

Then came my dada. And he was… every bit the man I thought he was. Imposing and daring. He died before any of us were even born, but I’ve heard stories of him. And he lived up to every single one of them.
The one that did not live up to his stories was Harun himself. My father.
Perhaps it is because I’ve heard of him as a young man, but never a boy. But the boy before me was anything but the man I know.

He convinced his father I was lost and scared, and my dada agreed to house me as long as everyone knew I wasn’t… a threat. He didn’t need to tell me what he meant, for I already knew he meant the Razakar’s, but he didn't know that term since they weren’t a thing until the following year. But I do. And I know what role they play.
I was still reeling back from everything that was happening around me when I found myself in new garments, courtesy of my two aunts who were now around my age or lesser.

I had no idea what to do after that. I was stuck here, in a time far off than my own, and I didn’t even know if it was a dream or if I could ever go back. But I didn’t have much time to myself, for just then, I felt that tiny tug on my hand again, only to look down at young Harun smiling up at me.
“Obai ao! Ekhta dekhaitham! (Come here! I want to show you something!)”
It wasn’t anything grand. Just a game him and his siblings were playing. Gulli danda.

He asked me if I knew how to play, to which I said no. He then went on to explain me the game in an excitement I had never seen in him, eyes lighting up with giddiness. The rest of them had gotten into some sort of quarrel, but my mejo sasa, the calmest of them all, turned to me and asked if I wanted to play, to which I denied again.

“Oisethe! Ar khelaithai nani!? (Enough! Are we not going to play anymore!?)” That was my suto fufu, the ever calm and cute lady that I remember her as. One yell from her and all her elder siblings were in formation, ready to start the game.

And my father lost in a matter of seconds. I found myself stifling a laughter as he came to slump down on the floor beside me, watching the rest of his siblings play. While he watched his siblings, I watched him, intrigued at the little boy before me.
There were a thousand questions in my head, a thousand things I wanted to tell him. But none of it would hold any weight, for this Harun had no idea who I was. I know him, but he does not know me.

And looking at him now as he is, I wondered to myself. If this is a side of him I had never gotten to see, a side he had hidden away from us so well, what more has he hidden from us to see? What more do we not know?
“H-Harun.?”
“Hmm?”
What do you want to be when you grow up? Should I ask him that? Or do you have any friends in Zakigonj? Do you ever wonder who you’ll marry? How many children will you have?
“Thumar kuno asha ase ni?”
Do you have any dreams?

Harun did not have to think long. It was like he has been waiting for someone to ask him that, the answer in the tip of his tongue. “Ase! Ami ekdin doctor bonmu! (There is! I want to be a doctor someday!)”
Oh.
You… wanted to be a doctor.
But he wasn’t done yet. It seemed like my question had opened a dam I didn’t know had so much water to flow out, with his eyes glittering in excitement as if he was already living that life.

“Ami bouth taka khomaimu. Boro bai o medical forra! Ami than lekan medical foriya ekhta boror doctor oimu! (I will earn a lot of money! Big brother is studying medicine as well! I will study the same and become a reputable doctor!)”
That is true. Boro sasa indeed studied medicine. He also became a rural doctor.
“Ar ami desh bidesh gurmu! Mojar mojar khani kaimu! Ice creamor lekan! (I will roam around the world! And I will taste delicious food! Like ice cream!)”
I chuckled despite myself.
“Er fore, ami abar goro aimu. Ar maizir lagi shundor shundor shari kinmu. Chok choki otha. (And then, I will come home again. And I will buy my mother pretty pretty sarees. The glittery ones.)”
No longer was his voice brimming with excitement, but a sort of calm belief, that the future was already in his hands. That it’d definitely come true.
Only that it never does.
And it’s not because of whatever happens next year. I know for a fact that he survives it, so the war doesn’t change the shape of his future. Something else does.
Harun is still smiling, but I can no longer smile along. I can only watch the boy I will one day call my father.
Because very soon, survival becomes your bigger concern than dreams, and the dreams you once saw become a luxury, so you choose to do things that will keep you afloat.
The Harun of today, doesn’t survive very long.
The you of today, disappears with the passing of time.
The Womanly Girl

I had no idea of the style of my coming here, or how anything worked. Because just as I found myself getting comfortable in this world, this world had other plans for me. As it turns out, it wasn’t done yet.
“Harun! Obai ao! Babai dakira! (Harun! Come here! Your father is summoning you!)”
Harun didn’t wait around or excuse himself the moment his mother hollered for him. Before I could even slip a word out of my mouth, he was up and running, leaving my outstretched hand adrift.
“W-Wait-”
But in all honesty, what could I even tell him?
Harun was gone, and so was everything else in my surroundings. And the next time I blinked, I was on my feet, in yet another familiar but unfamiliar place.
A lot remained the same here, unlike my dada bari.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”

A tiny little voice. So small I almost didn’t make it out through the thick thicket of trees. Dusk had already fallen, so it was a hassle making my way through the rickety pathway, leaves crunching under my feet as the pathway finally cleared, and before me was the house that had not aged a single day. Everything was still the same.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
A part of me already knew why I was here, but the closer I drew, and the clearer the little voice got, I found my breath hitching, especially when the owner of the voice finally came to my view.
There, on the veranda of my nana bari, sat a little girl no more than three, playing around with her collection of wooden dolls, repeating the same lines over and over again.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
Chubby and pudgy she was, with little pig tails on both sides of her head, cheeks flushed with giddy excitement over the two lines she had managed to learn.

I could not pinpoint the emotion that was brewing in me at the sight of her as I inched my way closer, until I was on my knees, earnestly looking at her delicate face that I had stared into my whole life, albeit older. The face of the woman she’d grow up to be.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
“Bou sajbe kal ki,” I found myself whispering, watching as her little head turned to look at me, chocolate brown eyes staring with curiosity as I continued. “Chorbe sonar palki.”

The woman that had helped me pack my bags during my first year at school, packed my lunch a thousand times over the years, was here right before me, unable to form a coherent sentence without anyone’s help.

Chocolate brown eyes collided with chocolate brown eyes, both filled with a tenderness that comes at certain ages. Mine was more on the sentimental side as I placed on a gentle smile, watching her doe like eyes scan my face.
“Thumar naam kita? (What’s your name?)” I found myself asking despite a part of me already knowing the answer. Yet, somehow, what the little girl before me said was not even on my mind.
“Shuela.”
Huh?
Isn’t it Fathima? Am I in the wrong pla-
Right.
Mother’s maiden name. The one her family remembered as. Shuela.
I chuckled despite myself, feeling the sudden bile rise up in my throat as if choking me with unwanted emotions.
My mother, like me, was a little girl too.
“Ino Khe!? (Who’s there!?)”
Thundered a voice, followed by countless footsteps. I flinched and moved away from the little girl, just as a woman rushed forward and pulled the girl into her arms, checking for injuries.

The man to whom the voice belonged glanced at his daughter and his wife who had grabbed her, before turning to me after making sure she was unharmed. “Afne khe, ar khare thukaira ino? (Who are you, and who are you looking for here?)”

Unlike my dada, my nana didn’t pretend he was alright with an intruder in his territory. Perhaps it was because my great grandfather himself was a Pakistani, so my dada was more open to housing strangers as a gesture of goodwill that he learnt from his father. The same couldn’t be told about my nana. And that was alright.
He was protecting his only child.
My mother, was loved too.
So what changed? What happened in your future that your family, this very family that protected you so much, turned away from you when you needed them the most?
Was it the birth of your sister? Or the children nana will have with his second wife? Did things as the eldest child change for you after that?
Or because you marry my father?
When do you lose this innocence?
Wake Up
Afa, utokka. Aichi.

I bowed my head in respect, clasping my hands in front of me before I began backtracking away from there. There was no point of saying anything to them. I was an intruder, and that alone was a red alert for them in that era. I should just leave.
So leave I did, but I was a fool to think it’d end there. Because now I could hear them throw chase.
“Oi! Thuin khe!? Ino kita khorre!? Oi! (Hey! Who are you!? What were you doing here!? Hey!)”
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
Shit.
I have to run away from here! I have to leave! I have to-
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
“Afa? Afa!”
I have to leave… I have to leave… I have to le-
“Afa! (Sister!)”

My eyes snapped open, a gasp escaping my lips as I finally felt air suck into my lungs like I had been deprived of it this whole time. My eyes fell on the man, the driver that was yelling for me to wake up.
The rickshaw driver. The middle-aged man. It was him this time.
“Amra aicchi. (We’ve arrived.)”
He was right. We did.
We have arrived at my dada bari.
In 2026 this time.
Epilogue

“Aicho ni? (You came?)” My mother’s voice was the first to greet me when I got back, but I said nothing, watching as she placed plates on the table for dinner while my father washed his hands to eat. It was him next. “Khaar goro khailai? (Whose house did you eat?)”
I replied to them after that. We ate, and they asked me mundane questions, and I replied. Like every other day. Only it no longer felt like every other day.
I look at my father, as if looking at him for the first time.
The boy who dreamt to be a doctor, to study medicine and then travel the world. To taste new things, and buy his mother pretty sarees.
Only that you never become one.

You never became a doctor, Harun. You never study medicine. You don’t travel the world, and you don’t really taste new things. And you see very less of your mother in the coming years before she passes away.

Fate had other plans for you, and it had nothing to do with the war that would follow the very next year after I saw you. You will grow up to become a bright young man, a pride of your mother and sisters. But not in the way you imagined.

You will travel to UAE because life in Bangladesh had nothing for you. But life in UAE ends up delivering more obstacles than you expected. Still, you fight through. You fight through, and you marry my mother. And you have us.
The dreams of the little boy from 1970 are pushed far back in the corner of your mind because keeping your new family thriving becomes your first priority. The sacrifice of a father.

I then turn to my mother. The girl who was once so loved and cherished by her parents, protected and sheltered. The girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. The ever-carefree child who grew up too fast.

Sooner than later you have a sister, and your parents will play favorites, until you are no longer the little girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. You become the shield that takes the blows for your siblings, the job of the eldest child. And over time, you experience as the shield child curves you into being the wife people expect you to be, a mother the generation deems a perfect fit.
And then you have us, and like father, we become your world. Like your siblings, we become the one in need of a shield. The sacrifice of a mother.
They all grew up too fast. The lines in their faces tell that story.
Somewhere along the way, youth left you behind, and we were born. We became your world, your priority. Being parents overrode the idea to be dreamers.
After all, you too, were just children with dreams, like us.

And perhaps it does not excuse the feeling of depravity of love that I felt as your child, or the reasons why you had favorites. It doesn’t explain why you could ask you other kids about their day and never mine until I was the last person left at home. Or why my presence in the house was always compared to that of my siblings. Never too much, never enough.
But it probably explains why you both are the way you both are.
You may not have fulfilled your childhood dreams, but you became the perfect parents.
So, now that I look at you, I know a little more.
The perfect mother and father. But not mom and dad.
And I guess, that is alright.
For there is no saying what future has in store for me too. If I too, will be expected to grow up fast. If I too, will be forced to push my dreams behind and become a responsible adult.
So, I guess, it is fine.
It is alright.
I know parts of you, and you know parts of me. But we can never know everything.
We are all strangers to one another somehow. Strangers that we know.
THE END

dada bari.

The baroi zao ekhon. Baade der oizibo.
(Then you better leave now, lest it becomes late.)” Were my father’s words to me, barely looking up from the phone in hand. But I could sense the concern edged in his voice.
I’m sure they loved me, but sometimes I can’t help but wonder if I was something they considered a gift, a choice, or a responsibility.
I pursed my lips before getting to my feet, smiling at them. “
Acha.
(Okay.)”
Because when you have a total of six children, the excitement of parenthood already disappears by the time the third or fourth child is born, let alone the sixth child.
Turning to look at my parents sitting across from one another, I knew exactly what they were.
The textbook versions of parents.
To be on Your Own

The journey to Beanibazar was definitely not an easy one, especially when one is traveling all the way from the city to the rural village. But I had to make it anyway. Starting from Shaporan I hailed an auto rickshaw that drove me till the bypass road, from where I then hailed yet another auto rickshaw that took me further inside only to drop me off at Gulapgonj. Every time I finished a trip, I found myself releasing a sigh of relief knowing that I was getting closer and closer without getting abducted or harassed. A girl can never be certain.

Yet, my journey was far from over, but close nonetheless. I was close to Narafing, and from here on, I could travel via manual rickshaw, which was the part I was looking forward to the most. Riding a rickshaw all by yourself with the wind brushing past your face as it speeds by was a welcoming thought, especially when it was the rural breeze of nature.
Kano zaitha?
(Where to?)” Asked the driver I had managed to hail. My reply was quick. “
Beanibazar sinoin ni?
(Do you know Beanibazar?)”
Beanibazar khe na sine?
(Who doesn’t know Beanibazar?)”
Right.
“Beanibazar, Ramdabazar,
Sondogram
?” My attempts at narrowing down my location was laughable. I was only saying names of places registered in my national ID at this point.
Khano, point o namba ni?
(Do you wish to be dropped on the main road?)”
Alright. Here goes nothing. “
Khan’s residence sinra ni?
(Do you know Khan’s residence?)”
Imagine my surprise when he said he does. This man was a god sent. I was finally saved from further embarrassment.
From then on, the ride was peaceful. The man took his sweet time riding towards my
dada bari
, while I leaned back and sighed in relief. I was indeed relieved, to the point I found myself feeling drowsy with leftover sleep.
This was not a wise idea, falling asleep in a rickshaw. But somehow, I found myself being lulled to a peaceful sleep, leaving my fate up to the heavens.

I don’t know for how long I slept, or if I had even slept to begin with. All I can say is I had just brushed my eyelids shut, maybe for a minute, or maybe a second, before I felt the rickshaw come to a stop.
Afa, utokka. Aicchi
. (Sister, wake up. We’re here.)”
Already?
My eyelids fluttered open, and true to his words, we had made it. I was right before the massive gates that led to my ancestral home, where my uncles and aunts were still there.
Only that something didn’t seem… right.
The gate seemed so… new. Like it was newly painted. Yet the paint was chipped, but the gate was in better condition than I had last seen it. And the place-
“Afa, bara dibani? (Sister, the fare?)”
Right. The fare- WOAH!
I almost flinched at the sight of the old man before me. Because up until a moment ago, it wasn’t an old man riding me.
Wasn’t it… a middle-aged man? Or did I get it wrong? Did I not look at his face enough?
But then… the rickshaw…
It was manual.
But I remember hailing a motor rickshaw.
What… is going on? Am I dreaming?
The Face of Unfamiliarity

Everything seemed to become a hazy mess before my eyes. I did not know how I paid the man and began making my way forward. All I knew was that my heart was in my throat, and my senses alert to the very strange and unfamiliar scent around me. Almost like it was… ancient.
Nothing felt familiar in this very familiar place. I remember there used to be a grocery shop outside the gates
Dola sasa
had made. Did they break it down? I don’t know. But the deeper I went, the stranger it got.
Because now I was finally seeing people around, people I call my family. But for some reason, most of them were… children. There were hardly any adults around.
The sound of laughter and giggles grew louder as I drew closer, making my way to a group of children playing on the mud. At the sight of me approaching them, their smiles faltered.
“H-Hi.” I greeted in English like the fool I was.
Silence.
Umm, ikta kita Khan residence ni?
(Is this Khan residence?)”
More silence. Until one of them turned to whisper something in another ear before they jumped to their feet and just like that, they took off. And all I could think was, did I say something wrong?

The kids were gone. Not just the kids I spoke to, but every other kid around as well. The whole place was vacant, like everyone had disappeared at the sight of me. I had no idea what was going on, or if there were any adults, but I needed to find answers. I needed to know where I was because this was certainly not my home. It looked like my home, but it wasn’t home.
“The renovations in
Boro sasa’s
house are gone. The study room
abbu
built in our house is gone too. In fact, the bedroom
abbu
built for
Moulana sasa

is gone too! And it was constructed two decades ago!” I stopped wherever I was going with a stomp of my foot, unable to believe what I had just seen. “How did everything disappear in less than a year!?”

And the more I think about it, the more it looks odd. I… could not recognize anyone. No matter how little I may have seen of them, I know who my relatives are! There is no way they all just disappeared into thin air and were replaced by children I never saw over there in my life!
So caught up in my train of thoughts, it takes me a while to realize I’m no longer in the Khan residence territory. I was somewhere else, like a rice field.
“Great. Now where the hell did I-”
Until I saw him. A young boy. In the rice field.

Sitting there all by himself, staring into the distance while being surrounded by cows and calves of all sizes. There he was, all alone in that massive watery field, with nothing but his cattle as company. And he looked so… peaceful.
Who are you? And why do you look so familiar?
I did not have long to dwell on it, because just then, my heart leaped out of my chest.
BANG!
The sound of gunfire.
I would be lying if I said I did not jump out of my skin when the shot was fired, followed by another, and another, until it was non stop.
“W-What… what is… what is going on… I-”
Words failed me, for fear had gripped me so hard I was rooted to my spot, unable to move. Tears burned my eyes making it harder to see, for I had no idea where I was, and now there were gunshots.
Could this day get any worse?
Just as I found myself resigning to my fate, I felt a tiny grip on my arm, yanking me towards them.
Ino ubai ruilai khene!? Lukao!
(Why are you just standing there!? Hide!)” It was the young boy from earlier.

I had no idea who he was, yet I found myself being dragged by him until we were both in the rice field, waist deep, before he sucked a breath and motioned for me to do the same. And like a child, I did as told.
And then, we dived in.
The Boy You Are

I don’t know how long we stayed under that murky water with rice plants all over us, but I knew one thing. The boy never let go of my hand. When we finally pulled up, the gunshots were gone. Like they never happened in the first place.
Was I imagining it? But the boy heard them too. Speaking of-

I coughed out whatever murk I may have swallowed, and so did the boy. But unlike my startled self, the boy looked entirely unfazed, like he was used to these things. But how come? This is the first time I’m hearing about a shootout in Beanibazar.
Dhuk faiso? (
Are you hurt?)”
I turned to the young boy looking up at me with his dark black eyes, unable to form any words. Because the more I looked at him, the familiar it got, until I was looking at someone else entirely.
A sudden gasp left my lips as I remembered something, looking at our surroundings. “
T-Thumar gai-
(Your cows-)”

But the boy only waved at me dismissively, something I noticed was an elderly gesture which this young man had learnt, before he whistled, and out came his herd from the water, having hidden just like us. Smart.
I smiled at the sight of the boy with his cows despite myself, until a thought struck me, my smile faltering immediately. This scene, I feel like I saw it somewhere. Or more like I heard it.
The boy that hid with his cows whenever there was a shootout.
The boy…
But that was impossible. What I was thinking. It was impossible. It couldn’t be.
I stared at the young boy smiling at his cows, the smile I had seen a handful of times, yet I could always recognize it.
Dorayona. Itha oe kunoshomoi.

(Don’t be afraid. This happens sometimes.)” I heard the boy say, confident in his words like it was not a big deal, or confident that he saved a life. But I could not bring myself to smile with him. For I found my heart shattering for this little boy.
He then went on to say, “
Thumar naam kitha? Harigeso?
(What’s your name? are you lost?)”
“J-J… Jerin.” I don’t know if I could tell him whether I was lost or not. But I needed to know something. But the boy was already talking, leading his cows out with him. “
Kuntha oitho nai. Amar loge ao. Amar babai thumare shahaijjo korba. Thain manshore shahaijjo dein.
(Don’t worry. Come with me. My dad will help you. He helps people like you.)”
The boy was already out and making his way towards the route I had come from, further registering my fears to be true. But I had to be sure.
So, I stopped the boy, finally ready to get some answers. “Chele, ami faurilaisi. E-Ekhon… kun bosor? (Boy, I have forgotten. W-What… year is it?)”
The boy looked at me judgmentally, but I couldn’t blame him. I really sounded like an idiot. But he answered nonetheless. And what he answered made my blood run cold.
Buligeso? Ekhon tho unnisho shottor
No…
“Forgotten it? It’s 1970.”
But if one bomb wasn’t enough. He dropped another.
Ar amar naam chele nai. Amar naam Harun.
“And my name is not boy. It’s Harun.”
The Man You Become

I ended up following the boy. Following… Harun. He promised me his father was very generous and would offer me shelter till I found my footing or even offer me a job. I didn’t argue. I already knew that.
I already knew what sort of man my grandfather was.
So Harun led me to his house, to… my
dada bari

. Where I had already come and found it awfully strange with unfamiliar faces. Only this time, there were more adult faces than children, and they gathered around Harun like he was lost. I mean he did survive a shootout.
After that, everything happened in a blur. Someone took the reins of the cows from him, and before he knew it he was surrounded by children around his age. Children I now recognize all too well.

My uncles and aunts. Boro sasa. Gura sasa. Dola sasa. Moulana sasa. Mejo fufu. Suto fufu. Mejo sasa. Suto sasa. All… young children. Boro fufu was the only one missing, perhaps because she was already married.

Then I saw dadi. My dadi, fit and well, rushing to her boy to see if he was unharmed. She was… pretty. I had never seen her like this. The only time I saw her alive was on her deathbed. And then she died.

Then came my dada. And he was… every bit the man I thought he was. Imposing and daring. He died before any of us were even born, but I’ve heard stories of him. And he lived up to every single one of them.
The one that did not live up to his stories was Harun himself. My father.
Perhaps it is because I’ve heard of him as a young man, but never a boy. But the boy before me was anything but the man I know.

He convinced his father I was lost and scared, and my dada agreed to house me as long as everyone knew I wasn’t… a threat. He didn’t need to tell me what he meant, for I already knew he meant the Razakar’s, but he didn't know that term since they weren’t a thing until the following year. But I do. And I know what role they play.
I was still reeling back from everything that was happening around me when I found myself in new garments, courtesy of my two aunts who were now around my age or lesser.

I had no idea what to do after that. I was stuck here, in a time far off than my own, and I didn’t even know if it was a dream or if I could ever go back. But I didn’t have much time to myself, for just then, I felt that tiny tug on my hand again, only to look down at young Harun smiling up at me.
“Obai ao! Ekhta dekhaitham!
(Come here! I want to show you something!)”
It wasn’t anything grand. Just a game him and his siblings were playing. Gulli danda.

He asked me if I knew how to play, to which I said no. He then went on to explain me the game in an excitement I had never seen in him, eyes lighting up with giddiness. The rest of them had gotten into some sort of quarrel, but my mejo sasa, the calmest of them all, turned to me and asked if I wanted to play, to which I denied again.
Oisethe! Ar khelaithai nani!?

(Enough! Are we not going to play anymore!?)” That was my suto fufu, the ever calm and cute lady that I remember her as. One yell from her and all her elder siblings were in formation, ready to start the game.

And my father lost in a matter of seconds. I found myself stifling a laughter as he came to slump down on the floor beside me, watching the rest of his siblings play. While he watched his siblings, I watched him, intrigued at the little boy before me.
There were a thousand questions in my head, a thousand things I wanted to tell him. But none of it would hold any weight, for this Harun had no idea who I was. I know him, but he does not know me.

And looking at him now as he is, I wondered to myself. If this is a side of him I had never gotten to see, a side he had hidden away from us so well, what more has he hidden from us to see? What more do we not know?
“H-Harun.?”
“Hmm?”
What do you want to be when you grow up? Should I ask him that? Or do you have any friends in Zakigonj? Do you ever wonder who you’ll marry? How many children will you have?
Thumar kuno asha ase ni?”
Do you have any dreams?
Harun did not have to think long. It was like he has been waiting for someone to ask him that, the answer in the tip of his tongue. “
Ase! Ami ekdin doctor bonmu!
(There is! I want to be a doctor someday!)”
Oh.
You… wanted to be a doctor.
But he wasn’t done yet. It seemed like my question had opened a dam I didn’t know had so much water to flow out, with his eyes glittering in excitement as if he was already living that life.
Ami bouth taka khomaimu. Boro bai o medical forra! Ami than lekan medical foriya ekhta boror doctor oimu!
(I will earn a lot of money! Big brother is studying medicine as well! I will study the same and become a reputable doctor!)”
That is true. Boro sasa indeed studied medicine. He also became a rural doctor.
Ar ami desh bidesh gurmu! Mojar mojar khani kaimu! Ice creamor lekan!
(I will roam around the world! And I will taste delicious food! Like ice cream!)”
I chuckled despite myself.
Er fore, ami abar goro aimu. Ar maizir lagi shundor shundor shari kinmu. Chok choki otha.
(And then, I will come home again. And I will buy my mother pretty pretty sarees. The glittery ones.)”
No longer was his voice brimming with excitement, but a sort of calm belief, that the future was already in his hands. That it’d definitely come true.
Only that it never does.
And it’s not because of whatever happens next year. I know for a fact that he survives it, so the war doesn’t change the shape of his future. Something else does.
Harun is still smiling, but I can no longer smile along. I can only watch the boy I will one day call my father.
Because very soon, survival becomes your bigger concern than dreams, and the dreams you once saw become a luxury, so you choose to do things that will keep you afloat.
The Harun of today, doesn’t survive very long.
The you of today, disappears with the passing of time.
The Womanly Girl

I had no idea of the style of my coming here, or how anything worked. Because just as I found myself getting comfortable in this world, this world had other plans for me. As it turns out, it wasn’t done yet.
Harun! Obai ao! Babai dakira!
(Harun! Come here! Your father is summoning you!)”
Harun didn’t wait around or excuse himself the moment his mother hollered for him. Before I could even slip a word out of my mouth, he was up and running, leaving my outstretched hand adrift.
“W-Wait-”
But in all honesty, what could I even tell him?
Harun was gone, and so was everything else in my surroundings. And the next time I blinked, I was on my feet, in yet another familiar but unfamiliar place.
A lot remained the same here, unlike my
dada bari.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”

A tiny little voice. So small I almost didn’t make it out through the thick thicket of trees. Dusk had already fallen, so it was a hassle making my way through the rickety pathway, leaves crunching under my feet as the pathway finally cleared, and before me was the house that had not aged a single day. Everything was still the same.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
A part of me already knew why I was here, but the closer I drew, and the clearer the little voice got, I found my breath hitching, especially when the owner of the voice finally came to my view.
There, on the veranda of my
nana bari
, sat a little girl no more than three, playing around with her collection of wooden dolls, repeating the same lines over and over again.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
Chubby and pudgy she was, with little pig tails on both sides of her head, cheeks flushed with giddy excitement over the two lines she had managed to learn.

I could not pinpoint the emotion that was brewing in me at the sight of her as I inched my way closer, until I was on my knees, earnestly looking at her delicate face that I had stared into my whole life, albeit older. The face of the woman she’d grow up to be.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
“Bou sajbe kal ki,”
I found myself whispering, watching as her little head turned to look at me, chocolate brown eyes staring with curiosity as I continued. “
Chorbe sonar palki.”

The woman that had helped me pack my bags during my first year at school, packed my lunch a thousand times over the years, was here right before me, unable to form a coherent sentence without anyone’s help.

Chocolate brown eyes collided with chocolate brown eyes, both filled with a tenderness that comes at certain ages. Mine was more on the sentimental side as I placed on a gentle smile, watching her doe like eyes scan my face.
Thumar naam kita?
(What’s your name?)” I found myself asking despite a part of me already knowing the answer. Yet, somehow, what the little girl before me said was not even on my mind.
“Shuela.”
Huh?
Isn’t it Fathima? Am I in the wrong pla-
Right.
Mother’s maiden name. The one her family remembered as. Shuela.
I chuckled despite myself, feeling the sudden bile rise up in my throat as if choking me with unwanted emotions.
My mother, like me, was a little girl too.
Ino Khe!?
(Who’s there!?)”
Thundered a voice, followed by countless footsteps. I flinched and moved away from the little girl, just as a woman rushed forward and pulled the girl into her arms, checking for injuries.
The man to whom the voice belonged glanced at his daughter and his wife who had grabbed her, before turning to me after making sure she was unharmed. “
Afne khe, ar khare thukaira ino?
(Who are you, and who are you looking for here?)”

Unlike my dada, my nana didn’t pretend he was alright with an intruder in his territory. Perhaps it was because my great grandfather himself was a Pakistani, so my dada was more open to housing strangers as a gesture of goodwill that he learnt from his father. The same couldn’t be told about my nana. And that was alright.
He was protecting his only child.
My mother, was loved too.
So what changed? What happened in your future that your family, this very family that protected you so much, turned away from you when you needed them the most?
Was it the birth of your sister? Or the children nana will have with his second wife? Did things as the eldest child change for you after that?
Or because you marry my father?
When do you lose this innocence?
Wake Up
Afa, utokka. Aichi.

I bowed my head in respect, clasping my hands in front of me before I began backtracking away from there. There was no point of saying anything to them. I was an intruder, and that alone was a red alert for them in that era. I should just leave.
So leave I did, but I was a fool to think it’d end there. Because now I could hear them throw chase.
Oi! Thuin khe!? Ino kita khorre!? Oi!
(Hey! Who are you!? What were you doing here!? Hey!)”
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
Shit.
I have to run away from here! I have to leave! I have to-
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
“Afa? Afa!”
I have to leave… I have to leave… I have to le-
Afa!
(Sister!)”

My eyes snapped open, a gasp escaping my lips as I finally felt air suck into my lungs like I had been deprived of it this whole time. My eyes fell on the man, the driver that was yelling for me to wake up.
The rickshaw driver. The middle-aged man. It was him this time.
Amra aicchi.
(We’ve arrived.)”
He was right. We did.
We have arrived at my
dada bari
In 2026 this time.
Epilogue

“Aicho ni? (You came?)” My mother’s voice was the first to greet me when I got back, but I said nothing, watching as she placed plates on the table for dinner while my father washed his hands to eat. It was him next. “Khaar goro khailai? (Whose house did you eat?)”
I replied to them after that. We ate, and they asked me mundane questions, and I replied. Like every other day. Only it no longer felt like every other day.
I look at my father, as if looking at him for the first time.
The boy who dreamt to be a doctor, to study medicine and then travel the world. To taste new things, and buy his mother pretty sarees.
Only that you never become one.

You never became a doctor, Harun. You never study medicine. You don’t travel the world, and you don’t really taste new things. And you see very less of your mother in the coming years before she passes away.

Fate had other plans for you, and it had nothing to do with the war that would follow the very next year after I saw you. You will grow up to become a bright young man, a pride of your mother and sisters. But not in the way you imagined.

You will travel to UAE because life in Bangladesh had nothing for you. But life in UAE ends up delivering more obstacles than you expected. Still, you fight through. You fight through, and you marry my mother. And you have us.
The dreams of the little boy from 1970 are pushed far back in the corner of your mind because keeping your new family thriving becomes your first priority. The sacrifice of a father.

I then turn to my mother. The girl who was once so loved and cherished by her parents, protected and sheltered. The girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. The ever-carefree child who grew up too fast.

Sooner than later you have a sister, and your parents will play favorites, until you are no longer the little girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. You become the shield that takes the blows for your siblings, the job of the eldest child. And over time, you experience as the shield child curves you into being the wife people expect you to be, a mother the generation deems a perfect fit.
And then you have us, and like father, we become your world. Like your siblings, we become the one in need of a shield. The sacrifice of a mother.
They all grew up too fast. The lines in their faces tell that story.
Somewhere along the way, youth left you behind, and we were born. We became your world, your priority. Being parents overrode the idea to be dreamers.
After all, you too, were just children with dreams, like us.

And perhaps it does not excuse the feeling of depravity of love that I felt as your child, or the reasons why you had favorites. It doesn’t explain why you could ask you other kids about their day and never mine until I was the last person left at home. Or why my presence in the house was always compared to that of my siblings. Never too much, never enough.
But it probably explains why you both are the way you both are.
You may not have fulfilled your childhood dreams, but you became the perfect parents.
So, now that I look at you, I know a little more.
The perfect mother and father. But not mom and dad.
And I guess, that is alright.
For there is no saying what future has in store for me too. If I too, will be expected to grow up fast. If I too, will be forced to push my dreams behind and become a responsible adult.
So, I guess, it is fine.
It is alright.
I know parts of you, and you know parts of me. But we can never know everything.
We are all strangers to one another somehow. Strangers that we know.
THE END

title: There’s a Man in the Woods.
author: wallflower
content: There's a man in the woods.
Haven't you heard?
There's a man in our woods.
He has lived here all his life;
Unwelcomed, feared, loathed.
We believe him to be a zealot; tainted.
He lives to remind us of his competence, insurgence.
"This is our land", "leave or perish", we tell him.
But he only shakes his bandaged head, holding firmly onto his crutches.
He sits by an Olive tree spending his days weaving Tatreez,
While listening to Ataaba on his rusty radio.
The sound of oud entices us indecently. What a rot to our souls!
Our children cannot help but follow the whimsies of the music.
We don't let them go any further;
Who knows what the man will do?
Who knows how he'll appeal?
He prays all the time to a god none of us recognize.
The elders say he curses us,
That he plots against us in our sleep,
They say he is the devils' apparition.
His belief, his practices are evidence enough,
He isn't one of us.
So, he isn't human to us.
There's a man in our woods
He's been here all his life.
He claims our land,
But we will give him a fight.
Don't you dare consider him,
Don't you dare sympathize.
There's thousands of us, only one of him
In the black of the night, we set the woods on fire,
The blazing red amidst the forest green,
And the man in the midst of it all stands,
Wearing a white thobe, head held high.
There's thousands of us, only one of him.
"But why do I feel bad?"
That's what he wants you to feel, yeled.
He plays with your mind.
"How do I stop?'
Stop feeling.
Stop the little twists of your heart.
Be strong.
"To be strong means to be heartless?"
Something revolts inside me, I force out a yes.
There's a man in our woods
And we hate him because no matter how hard we try-
He stays.
And in the quietness of our own failure,
We hear our hearts falter and miss a few beats,
And we don't see our reflection in the water, we only see malevolence.
Someone pulled at the loose ends of humanity's apparel and it came undone
Only to reveal the depravity of deceit.
Between the hours of conscience and cruelty there's a gap in time,
I call it dawn.
I approach the man
And ask him one question,
"Why do you persist?"
He smiles tenderly,
"Iman."
There's a man in the woods.
excerpt: A poem that places an uncanny presence at the edge of the woods.

title: The Cave
author: Nabila Anjum
content: Dear ___,
I’m writing to you because anytime now I’ll forgive you.
But she abandoned me!
Your actions made me feel abandoned because they used to make me feel accepted, but my feelings, valid they may be, are nobody’s responsibility but mine.

Your quick goodbye before moving to the other half of the planet had yet to hit me, so I pretended to understand when you said, “It took a lot of waiting,” while rushing to a goodbye like you didn’t see the opportunity coming.

There might have been uncertainty, but I thought we shared our uncertainties. Slowly I realized I wasn’t someone you talked about the things that mattered to you, rather about the things that distracted you from what mattered. I treat my cigarette that way; it’s no way of treating a friend. A friend is not an immediate source of low pleasure, merely someone to idle talk with, so you- now having quenched your thirst for shallowness- can dive deep into your solitude to do the real talking to yourself. Friendship is not a means to an end. Friendship is the end.
But anytime now I will forgive you.
She was busy.

Yes, you probably were. You must have been overwhelmed by the details of a new space, a new time zone; you must have been overstimulated all day and exhausted by the end of the day. Then again, aren’t you always? Is your hypervigilance a response to your surroundings, or a predisposition? I can tell because I share this predisposition.

No matter where we are- home or abroad- we are… in a cave. We are always in the survival mode. We believe we are more in danger than the people around us, so we feel entitled to use them as a means to our safety. Although the safety is imagined like the danger, unlike the constant danger, the safety is fleeting. That is, no one has ever made us feel safe for long enough, so we feel entitled to dispose of them until, I too, have been disposed of.
But anytime now I will forgive you and never write to you anymore because I’m trying to dismantle the cave, which we used to have our idle talks in, and subvert the survival mode that we bonded over.
Sincerely-
